nodes.title: The Census: Israel Arrayed Around the Presence
nodes.summary: Numbers opens with counting: the fighting men tribe by tribe, then the camp laid out in ranks with the tabernacle at dead center and the Levites ringed around it as a guard. The lists read dry until their design appears, a nation being shaped into marching order with God's dwelling in the middle and every tribe assigned its place and its load. The Levites are counted separately, taken in place of Israel's firstborn and given the sanctuary's care, so that nearness to holiness protects the camp instead of destroying it.
key_themes: Levites in place of the firstborn

prerequisites.reason: The camp is organized around the tabernacle Exodus just completed; the cloud that fills it now leads the march.

nodes.discussion_prompt: Every tribe in this camp knows exactly where it stands, and every position is defined by its relation to the tent at the center. If someone mapped your week the way Numbers 2 maps the camp, what would sit at the center of the layout, and how did it get there?
assessment_questions: Who gets counted in the census of Numbers 1, who is left out of it, and what different assignment are the uncounted given?
The same people are counted like an army and arranged like a congregation around God's tent. What is that double identity preparing Israel to be?

Every Israelite in these chapters has an assigned place and an assigned burden, down to who carries which pole. What place and load have been given to you in your family or community, and what would carrying them the way chapter 4 describes look like?

teaching_concepts.concept: A census in service of promise
teaching_concepts.explanation: The count musters the people God multiplied in Egypt for the march to the land he swore, so even a muster roll is covenant bookkeeping, promise turned into organization.
The camp's geometry preaches: God's dwelling in the middle, every tribe oriented toward it, and all order flowing outward from the holy.

teaching_concepts.concept: The Levites as substitutes and shield
teaching_concepts.explanation: Taken in place of the firstborn God claimed at the exodus, the Levites absorb the danger of nearness and keep wrath from the people, service framed as protection.
The careful wrapping and carrying rules of chapter 4 treat the holy things as lethal to casual contact, teaching reverence through procedure rather than sentiment.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain what the census and camp layout of Numbers 1-2 are for, and describe the double role the Levites play between the tabernacle and the tribes.

comprehension_check.question: Numbers 1-2 spends two chapters on head counts and camp positions. What are the lists doing?
options: Preserving the tax and supply records of the wilderness years
Proving the exodus account with verifiable population figures
Ranking the twelve tribes by the honor each had earned
Forming a people into an ordered camp around God's dwelling
comprehension_check.why: Numbers 2:2 gives the design: every tribe camped under its own banner around the Tent of Meeting, a nation taking its shape from the presence at its center.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Numbers 2:1-2 and Numbers 2:17. Notice where the Tent travels when the whole camp moves.

comprehension_check.question: Why are the Levites pulled out of the military census and camped in a ring around the tabernacle?
options: They replace the firstborn and shield the camp from wrath
They form an elite corps holier than the other tribes
They are exempted so that worship never pauses for war
They earn the position by stricter obedience to the law
comprehension_check.why: Numbers 3:12-13 and Numbers 1:53 give both halves: God takes the Levites in place of Israel's firstborn, and their camp keeps wrath from the congregation.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Numbers 3:11-13 for whose place the Levites take, then Numbers 1:53 for what their position prevents.

nodes.title: The Camp Consecrated and the March from Sinai
nodes.summary: Before Israel can march, the camp must be fit for the God at its center: purity regulations, restitution for wrongs, and the Nazirite vow press holiness into ordinary relationships. At the heart of the section God puts his own name on the people in the priestly blessing, and the tribes answer with twelve days of identical offerings for the altar's dedication. Passover is kept, with provision made for the unclean and the far away to keep it late, and when the cloud lifts, Israel finally moves out from Sinai behind the ark with the trumpets sounding.
key_themes: a camp fit for God's presence

prerequisites.reason: The consecration and departure assume the camp already censused and arrayed around the tabernacle.

nodes.discussion_prompt: The priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24-26 asks God to bless, keep, shine, be gracious, turn his face, and give peace, spoken over people about to walk into a wilderness. Why do you think Israel is given these words at this moment, and which line would you most need spoken over you this week?
assessment_questions: What does God instruct Aaron and his sons to do for Israel in Numbers 6:22-27, and what does he say the act places on the people?
Numbers 7 records the identical offering twelve times over when a single summary would have done. What might the repetition be saying about the tribes and the altar?

Israel's travel schedule in Numbers 9:15-23 has no fixed itinerary, only a cloud that lifts or settles. Which decision in front of you right now most needs that posture of readiness to wait or move, and what would practicing it look like?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The section moves holiness out of the sanctuary into the camp's relationships, wrongs repaid and vows kept, insisting that life around God's dwelling answers to him in its details.
Numbers 6:27 says the spoken blessing puts God's own name on Israel, so the people's security rides on who God is, pronounced over them again and again.
Chapter 7 records the same offering twelve times over, giving every tribe identical standing at the altar and showing that God receives each giver singly rather than in bulk.
The cloud, the trumpets, and the ark going ahead make God himself the itinerary, so Israel's only schedule is attentiveness.

nodes.completion_criteria: Describe what the priestly blessing asks and what Numbers 6:27 says it places on Israel, and explain how the cloud and the trumpets governed the march from Sinai.

comprehension_check.question: Numbers 5-9 fills the space between the census and the departure with purity rules, vows, blessing, and offerings. What is this material doing there?
options: Setting conditions Israel must meet to earn the land
Making the camp fit to carry God's presence on the road
Recording miscellaneous laws with no bearing on the story
Teaching sound hygiene for a large camp in a harsh wilderness
comprehension_check.why: Numbers 5:3 states the logic at the outset: the camp must be kept clean because the LORD himself dwells in the middle of it.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Numbers 5:1-4 and notice the reason given at the end of the paragraph for moving the unclean outside.

comprehension_check.question: What does the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:22-27 actually give Israel?
options: A formula whose recitation guarantees safety on the march
A prayer priests may speak only over the deserving
God's own name and favor, set on the people
A privilege kept for the priests and their households
comprehension_check.why: Numbers 6:27 explains the gift beneath the words: the blessing puts God's name on the Israelites, and God himself does the blessing.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Numbers 6:22-27 to the last verse. Notice who acts once the priests have finished speaking.

nodes.title: Rebellion at the Edge of the Land

comprehension_check.question: Ten spies and two see the same land, the same cities, the same giants (Numbers 13). What actually divides the two reports?
options: Whether the land is as rich as the promise claimed
Whether Israel's forces need more training before an assault
Whether God's promise gets any weight in the assessment
Whether the giants are as large as the majority insists
comprehension_check.why: Numbers 14:8-9 grounds the minority report in the LORD's presence and pleasure, the factor the ten never mention.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Numbers 13:30-33 and 14:6-9 again. Notice what Caleb and Joshua bring up that the ten never do.

comprehension_check.question: In Numbers 14 God pardons the people at Moses' plea, yet that generation still dies outside the land. How do the two outcomes fit?
options: Forgiveness stands while the refusal still carries its cost
The pardon was withdrawn again at the very next complaint
Moses won only a stay of execution rather than pardon
The people were spared and only the ten spies punished
comprehension_check.why: Numbers 14:20-23 places the word of pardon and the closed door side by side in a single reply.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Numbers 14:20-23 and 14:34 again. Notice what God grants Moses and what he still swears.

nodes.summary: Grumbling escalates to catastrophe: twelve spies scout Canaan, ten spread fear, and the people refuse to enter. The generation of the Exodus is sentenced to die in the wilderness — forty years for forty days of faithless scouting.

prerequisites.reason: The grumbling motif begun after the sea crossing now reaches its breaking point at Kadesh.

Numbers' account of Israel's refusal to enter Canaan presumes the reader knows the Abrahamic promise of land to Abraham and his seed as the covenantal basis for God's claim and Israel's vocation, a promise Genesis 12–17 supplies but Numbers does not recount in full.

connections.reason: Hebrews 3-4 turns the Kadesh refusal into the standing warning: 'Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.'
Psalms 95 and 106 retell this rebellion as Israel's cautionary self-portrait.

nodes.discussion_prompt: Twelve spies walk the same land and come back with two different verdicts. What lets Caleb and Joshua look at the same giants and see promise where the other ten see doom, and what would trusting God's promise over your fear cost you today?
assessment_questions: What do the twelve spies report about Canaan, and how do the people respond?
Moses pleads for Israel by quoting God's own words about his slow anger and steadfast love. Why does his intercession appeal to God's character instead of the people's record?

The people talk themselves into believing slavery in Egypt was better than the risk of trusting God. Where do you romanticize an old comfort instead of stepping toward what God has put in front of you?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Israel's refusal to trust God's promise at Kadesh costs an entire generation the land, showing that faith is a decision with stakes.
God hears Moses' intercession and pardons the people, yet the consequences of their refusal still stand, so forgiveness and discipline belong to the same God.
Moses intercedes for the very people who exhaust him, and God spreads the load onto seventy elders, showing that spiritual leadership is weight-bearing work.
The grumbling people remember Egypt as a place of free fish rather than slavery, showing how fear distorts the past to excuse distrust in the present.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell the story of the twelve spies and explain why that one refusal at Kadesh cost the Exodus generation the promised land.

nodes.title: Korah's Revolt and the Contested Priesthood

comprehension_check.question: Korah's slogan in Numbers 16:3 sounds true, since the whole congregation is holy. Why does the story treat it as rebellion?
options: It denies that ordinary Israelites carry any holiness at all
It insults Moses, and insulting God's servant is punished
It demands that the priesthood be abolished for everyone
It uses a shared truth to grab a God-given role
comprehension_check.why: Numbers 16:11 names the real target, a company gathered against the LORD who assigned the priesthood.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Numbers 16:8-11 again. Notice whom Moses says the company has actually banded against.

comprehension_check.question: After the revolt, the unit turns to a preserved staff, priestly duties, and the red heifer's ashes (Numbers 17-19). What is this material for?
options: Replacing worship at the tent with tighter crowd control
Settling who mediates, and keeping a death-marked camp near God
Rewarding the tribe of Levi with income for its loyalty
Teaching that death no longer defiles those inside the covenant
comprehension_check.why: Numbers 17:10 keeps the staff to end the grumbling, and Numbers 19:9 keeps cleansing ready where death keeps touching.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Numbers 17:10 and 19:9 again. Notice what each kept object is for once the crisis passes.

nodes.summary: Korah leads a revolt against Moses and Aaron — 'all the congregation is holy, why do you exalt yourselves?' — and the earth swallows the rebels. Aaron's staff buds to settle whose priesthood God has chosen, and the red heifer rite addresses death's contamination.

prerequisites.reason: Korah's challenge is an attack on the Aaronic priesthood established in Leviticus; the stakes are invisible without it.
The revolt grows out of the despair following the wilderness sentence.

connections.reason: Jude cites 'Korah's rebellion' as a byword for defying God-given authority.

nodes.discussion_prompt: Korah's slogan sounds almost right: the whole congregation is holy, so why should Moses and Aaron stand above it? What does the story suggest went wrong in how he used that truth, and how do you tell the difference between serving God and grasping at a role God has not given you?
assessment_questions: What happens to Korah and his followers, and how does God then settle whose priesthood he has chosen?
When the plague breaks out, Aaron runs into the middle of it with incense and stands between the dead and the living. What does that scene teach about what a mediator is for?

Korah was already a Levite with real, God-given work to do, yet he wanted more. Where does envy of someone else's role creep into your life, and what would contentment with your own calling look like?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The earth swallowing Korah shows that defying the order God has established is a serious matter rather than a mere leadership dispute.
Aaron's staff budding overnight settles the priesthood question with a sign from God, so the community can trust that its mediators serve by appointment rather than ambition.

teaching_concepts.concept: God supplies the remedy for death
teaching_concepts.explanation: The red heifer rite treats contact with death as real defilement and shows that only God can provide the cleansing for it.
The tassels commanded in Numbers 15 turn obedience into a daily visual habit, keeping God's commands in view rather than leaving them to memory alone.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell Korah's revolt and its outcome, and explain how Aaron's budding staff and his stand between the dead and the living answer the question of who mediates for Israel.

nodes.title: The Bronze Serpent and Balaam

comprehension_check.question: In Numbers 21:8-9 the cure for the serpent bites is a look at the bronze serpent on the pole. What is the passage teaching through that arrangement?
options: Healing comes through trusting the remedy God appoints
The bronze image held a power Israel could keep using
The serpent's own spirit had to be ritually appeased
God healed the few whose faith was already strong
comprehension_check.why: Numbers 21:8 promises life to any bitten person who looks, so the power sits in God's word behind the sign.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Numbers 21:8-9 again. Notice what the bitten must do, and how little it is.

comprehension_check.question: Balak's hired curses fail across Numbers 22-24, yet Israel is devastated in Numbers 25. What does that sequence reveal?
options: The blessings lapsed once the seer was paid and gone
Moab's gods proved stronger at Peor than on the heights
No outside curse can do what Israel's own sin can
God's protection ended when Moses struck the rock in anger
comprehension_check.why: Numbers 23:8 shows the hired curse powerless, and Numbers 25:1-3 shows the wound arriving from inside the camp.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Numbers 23:8 and 25:1-3 again. Notice where the real damage finally comes from.

nodes.summary: Moses strikes the rock and forfeits the land; a bronze serpent lifted on a pole heals all who look at it; and the pagan seer Balaam, hired to curse Israel, can only bless — prophesying a star from Jacob. Victory sours at Peor when Israel curses itself through idolatry.

prerequisites.reason: These are the closing events of the condemned generation's forty years.

connections.reason: Jesus makes the bronze serpent the picture of his own lifting up: 'as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness…' (John 3:14).
Balaam's 'star out of Jacob' stands behind the star the magi follow.

nodes.discussion_prompt: Everyone bitten by the serpents was offered the same cure: look at the bronze serpent lifted on the pole and live. Why do you think God chose a remedy that asked for nothing except a look of trust, and what does that say about how rescue from sin works?
assessment_questions: What does Moses do at the rock in Meribah, and what consequence does God announce for him?
Balaam is hired to curse Israel and finds he can only bless. What does his story reveal about whether God's purposes can be bought or turned aside?

Israel survives every enemy army in these chapters and then falls to temptation at Peor. Why is quiet compromise often more dangerous than open opposition, and where does that warning land in your life?

teaching_concepts.concept: Leaders answer for how they represent God
teaching_concepts.explanation: Moses strikes the rock in anger instead of speaking as commanded, and the cost of misrepresenting God before the people is losing entry to the land.

teaching_concepts.concept: A saving sign that points forward
teaching_concepts.explanation: The bronze serpent heals everyone who simply looks in trust, and Jesus later names it as the picture of his own lifting up on the cross.

teaching_concepts.concept: Blessing that cannot be hired away
teaching_concepts.explanation: Balaam's oracles show that God's commitment to bless his people overrides money, kings, and professional curses.
The failure at Peor shows that a people no army could defeat can still defeat itself by embracing idolatry and immorality.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell the bronze serpent episode and explain both why Moses was barred from the land and what Balaam's oracles reveal about God's unstoppable blessing.

nodes.title: The Second Census and the Succession
nodes.summary: After the plague at Peor, a new census counts a new Israel: the generation born in the wilderness, mustered on the plains of Moab for the land their parents refused. The count settles how the land will be divided, and its fairness is immediately tested when the five daughters of Zelophehad claim their dead father's portion and God rules in their favor. Moses, told he will see the land only from a mountain, asks God for a shepherd to replace him, and Joshua is commissioned in public before the priest and the whole assembly.

prerequisites.reason: The new census follows the plague at Peor and formally closes the Exodus generation's story.

connections.reason: Joshua's commissioning here is the hinge into the conquest narrative.

nodes.discussion_prompt: Moses hears he will die outside the land, and his first recorded response in Numbers 27:15-17 is a request that the people not be left leaderless. What does that moment reveal about Moses, and what would wanting your work to outlive you that way look like in practice?
assessment_questions: What does Numbers 26:64-65 record about who from the first census is still present in the second, and why?

The daughters of Zelophehad bring a case no existing law covers, and God says their claim is just. What does the way their case is received and answered show about the character of the law being given?

Moses hands his authority to Joshua in public, hands laid on him before the priest and the assembly in Numbers 27:22-23. What is worth imitating in how Moses lets go of his life's work, and where might you be holding something God is asking you to hand on?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The second census counts a nation that did not exist at Sinai, quiet proof that judgment on the parents did not cancel the covenant with the children.
Unlike the first muster, this count is expressly for dividing the land, so the list works like a title deed written in advance, promise treated as fact.
The Zelophehad ruling shows Israel's law able to hear an uncovered case and correct toward justice, with God himself affirming the claim of the overlooked.
Moses asks for a successor in shepherd language and commissions Joshua publicly, modeling authority that seeks the flock's good beyond its own tenure.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain what makes the second census different in purpose from the first, and describe how the Zelophehad ruling and Joshua's commissioning each prepare Israel for the land.

comprehension_check.question: Numbers 26 repeats the census of chapter 1 with a new generation. What is the second count for?
options: Fixing each tribe's share of the land ahead
Measuring the nation's decline across the wilderness years
Confirming the army's recovery after the plague at Peor
Replacing muster records lost during the forty years
comprehension_check.why: Numbers 26:52-56 draws the conclusion straight from the count: the land is to be apportioned among these names, larger and smaller by their numbers.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Numbers 26:52-56, the instruction that follows the counting. Notice what the totals are immediately used for.

comprehension_check.question: What does the scene of Numbers 27:12-23 establish about leadership in Israel?
options: Authority passes by seniority to the eldest qualified elder
Each leader should name his own son to guard the legacy
The office ends with Moses, since no one could replace him
God appoints the shepherd, and the handover happens in the open
comprehension_check.why: Numbers 27:18-23 has God name Joshua and Moses commission him before Eleazar and all the congregation, succession given from above and sealed in public.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Numbers 27:15-23. Notice who chooses the successor and who is watching when authority changes hands.

nodes.title: The Offerings Calendar and the Law of Vows
nodes.summary: With the land in view, God fixes Israel's calendar: the daily offerings morning and evening, then Sabbaths, new moons, and the festival cycle from Passover to Tabernacles, each with its prescribed gifts. The rhythm is relentless on purpose, a nation's time claimed hour by hour and season by season for the God it serves. Chapter 30 then turns from public worship to private speech, binding vows and oaths with rules for when a word must stand and who can release it, because a people whose worship is ordered must also mean what it says.

prerequisites.reason: The offerings calendar is delivered to the generation just censused on the plains of Moab.

nodes.discussion_prompt: This calendar starts with two offerings every single day before it ever reaches a festival, and the great feasts stand on top of that steady base. Looking at how your own weeks and years are patterned, what does your calendar say you are devoted to, and what would a daily base layer of devotion change?
assessment_questions: What offering opens the calendar in Numbers 28:3-8, and what is its schedule?
The festival list piles daily, weekly, monthly, and yearly rhythms on top of one another. What is a calendar like this designed to do to a people's sense of time?

Numbers 30 treats a spoken vow as something that binds, releasable only through defined relationships and never through convenience. What promise are you currently tempted to quietly downgrade, and what would this chapter's seriousness about words ask of you there?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The calendar builds devotion into time itself, daily offerings under weekly, monthly, and yearly feasts, so covenant loyalty becomes a practiced pattern rather than a periodic burst.
Everything festal rests on the morning and evening offering that never lapses, teaching that extraordinary worship grows out of ordinary constancy.
Numbers 28:2 has God call the offerings and their times his own, framing the year as a series of appointments God himself has set.
Numbers 30:2 binds a person to his word because Israel's God keeps his, and the chapter's careful release rules treat spoken words as weighty enough to need law at all.

nodes.completion_criteria: Describe the layers of Israel's worship calendar from daily to yearly, and explain what Numbers 30 teaches about the weight of a spoken vow.

comprehension_check.question: Numbers 28-29 schedules offerings for every day, week, month, and feast of the year. What is the calendar for?
options: Funding the sanctuary's needs through a predictable stream of gifts
Securing good harvests by keeping God continually satisfied
Claiming the whole shape of Israel's time for the LORD
Testing the nation's obedience through sheer ritual demand
comprehension_check.why: Numbers 28:2 sets the frame: these are the LORD's offerings at the LORD's appointed times, so the calendar belongs to him before it belongs to Israel.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Numbers 28:1-2 and Numbers 29:39. Notice whose appointed times the whole list keeps calling these.

comprehension_check.question: Why does the law of vows in Numbers 30 sit beside the offerings calendar?
options: So worshipers would know which offerings each kind of vow requires
Words offered to God bind like offerings brought to him
It quietly steers Israel away from ever making vows
Private promises outrank the public duties of the feasts
comprehension_check.why: Numbers 30:2 gives a vow the same seriousness as an altar gift: what leaves the lips for God must be carried out.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Numbers 30:1-2 right after Numbers 29:39-40. Notice how the subject shifts from what Israel offers to what Israel says.

nodes.title: Last Acts in Moab: Midian, Transjordan, and the Map of the Land
nodes.summary: The wilderness account closes with unfinished business and forward motion: vengeance on Midian for Peor, a hard chapter that refuses to soften Israel's story, then the Transjordan tribes winning their request on the condition that they fight for their brothers first. An itinerary recounts the whole road from Egypt stage by stage. Then the land not yet entered is bounded, allotted, and legislated, with towns for the Levites, refuge for the accused, and a final ruling for Zelophehad's daughters, so that Numbers ends with a map of promises drawn as if the crossing were already done.

prerequisites.reason: The closing acts in Moab resume the narrative after the calendar and vow laws.

nodes.discussion_prompt: Numbers 33 walks back through roughly forty stops on the road from Egypt, most of them places where nothing recorded happened. Why do you think Israel was told to keep the whole list, and what would your own list of stops look like if you wrote out the last decade that way?
assessment_questions: What condition do Reuben and Gad accept in Numbers 32 before they may settle east of the Jordan?

Chapters 34-36 spend their energy on boundaries, Levite towns, and refuge cities for a land Israel has not entered. What does legislating in advance say about how this generation is meant to regard the promise?

Moses warns in Numbers 32:23 that walking away from their brothers' battles would be sin with a way of catching up to them. Where does your own comfort tempt you to settle early while others still fight for theirs, and what would keeping the Numbers 32 bargain look like for you?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The Transjordan grant binds settlement to solidarity, the first tribes seated only on condition that they arm for the rest, making inheritance a shared project.
The cities of refuge put due process into geography, shielding the accidental killer from vengeance until trial, so mercy and justice are zoned into the land before Israel arrives.
Numbers 35:34 grounds the land law in God's own dwelling among the Israelites, so how they treat blood, boundaries, and neighbors is a matter of hosting his presence.
The itinerary of chapter 33 fixes the whole wilderness road in Israel's memory, each stage a receipt of survival, before the command to take the land in Numbers 33:53.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain the condition attached to the Transjordan settlement, what the cities of refuge are for, and why Numbers ends by mapping and legislating a land not yet entered.

comprehension_check.question: Numbers ends with boundary lines, city lists, and inheritance rulings for territory still across the river. What does that ending assert?
options: The coming conquest will succeed through Israel's military readiness
The wilderness generation finally earned the land by patience
Careful planning will keep Israel from losing heart again
The grant is certain enough to be surveyed unseen
comprehension_check.why: Numbers 33:53 rests the whole section on God's word: the land is given, therefore Israel is to take possession and settle it.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Numbers 33:50-54 and Numbers 34:1-2. Notice how the LORD speaks of the land before anyone has crossed the river.

comprehension_check.question: Why does the law of Numbers 35 set aside cities of refuge in the middle of the tribal allotments?
options: So bloodshed is weighed at trial, ahead of the avenger
So killers of any kind can purchase asylum from the Levites
So the Levite towns gain standing and support among the tribes
So violent men can be banished without more blood being shed
comprehension_check.why: Numbers 35:12 states the purpose: the cities shield the accused from the avenger until he stands before the congregation for judgment.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Numbers 35:9-15 and Numbers 35:24-25. Notice who the refuge protects and what must happen before any case is settled.
